cards.front: What is a [[kw:point estimate]] for the population mean $\mu$?
back: A single value estimate. The best point estimate of $\mu$ is the [[imp:sample mean]] $\bar{x}$.
$\bar{x}$ is an unbiased estimator — its average over all possible samples equals $\mu$.
It gives a range of plausible values for $\mu$, reflecting sampling variability.
A point estimate alone gives no indication of precision.
cards.front: Why is an [[kw:interval estimate]] better than a point estimate?
Define the [[kw:margin of error]] $E$ for a large‑sample confidence interval for $\mu$.
back: The maximum likely difference between $\bar{x}$ and $\mu$.

cards.front: Give the critical values $z_c$ for 90%, 95%, and 99% confidence.
back: These z‑scores capture the middle area $c$ of the standard normal distribution.
Also written $\bar{x} \pm E$ or $(\bar{x} - E,\, \bar{x} + E)$.
cards.front: Write the large‑sample [[kw:confidence interval for $\mu$]].

back: 95% CI: $(114.4, 147.2)$. We are 95% confident $\mu$ lies in this interval.
If we take many samples and build a 95% CI from each, about [[imp:95% of them]] will contain $\mu$.
We do NOT say “there is a 95% chance $\mu$ is in this interval.”
cards.front: Interpret a 95% confidence interval correctly.

back: Use $s$ as an estimate of $\sigma$. [[imp:Always round up]] to the next whole number.

How does increasing the confidence level affect the width of a confidence interval?
back: Example: 99% CI is wider than 95% CI for the same data.

cards.front: How does increasing the sample size affect the margin of error?
back: This yields a narrower, more precise interval.

cards.front: When can you use $s$ in place of $\sigma$ in the z‑interval formula?
back: The sampling distribution of $\bar{x}$ is approximately normal, and $s$ is a good estimate of $\sigma$.

When should you use a [[kw:t‑distribution]] instead of the normal distribution for a CI for $\mu$?
back: When $\sigma$ is [[imp:unknown]] and the sample size is small ($n < 30$).
The population must be approximately normally distributed.
2. [[imp:Thicker tails]] than the standard normal distribution.
3. The exact shape depends on the degrees of freedom: $d.f. = n-1$.
As $d.f.$ increase, the t‑distribution approaches the standard normal.

back: We are 95% confident the true mean temperature is between 156.7°F and 167.3°F.

Construct a 99% t‑CI for days on a car lot: $n=20$, $\bar{x}=9.75$, $s=2.39$.
back: We are 99% confident the true mean days on the lot is between 8.22 and 11.28.
The t‑distribution has thicker tails, so $t_c > z_c$ for the same confidence level.
A larger critical value gives a larger margin of error, hence a wider interval.
This extra width accounts for the uncertainty of estimating $\sigma$ with $s$.

What condition must be checked before using a t‑interval for a small sample?
back: The population must be [[imp:approximately normally distributed]].
If the population is heavily skewed and $n$ is small, the t‑interval is not valid.
When the sample size is [[imp:at least 30]] ($n \ge 30$).
The Central Limit Theorem ensures normality, and $s$ is a good substitute for $\sigma$.
cards.front: When can you use a z‑interval even if $\sigma$ is unknown?
Decide which distribution to use: $n=25$, $\sigma$ unknown, population normal.
back: If $\sigma$ were known, we could use z.

cards.front: Decide which distribution to use: $n=45$, $\sigma$ unknown, any population.
back: $n=45 \ge 30$ → use the [[kw:normal (z) distribution]] with $s$ in place of $\sigma$.
The CLT ensures the sampling distribution is approximately normal.
